positions/african-spiritual-warfare/name: African Christian theologies of spirits and power
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/oneL: African Christians commonly inhabit a world in which ancestors, spirits and witchcraft are real; the gospel is received as Christ’s supreme power over all such forces, bringing protection, healing and freedom from fear, expressed through prayer, prophecy and deliverance.
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/core: The spiritual world is real and affects health, fertility and fortune.
Christ is victor over all powers (Colossians 2:15) — for some, the supreme ancestor.
Missionary Christianity often ignored these realities, so African churches had to address them.
Deliverance, healing and protection are integral to salvation.
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/orig: Visible in prophet movements (William Wade Harris, 1913; Garrick Braide; Simon Kimbangu, 1921), Aladura churches (1930), Ethiopian Orthodox and Catholic healing ministries (Milingo), and African Pentecostalism; theorised by Kwame Bediako, Ogbu Kalu and Opoku Onyinah.
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/stro: It takes the biblical world of powers seriously, closer to the New Testament than Western rationalism.
It addresses the felt needs and fears of ordinary believers.
It has driven the explosive growth of African Christianity.

Critics (including African theologians) warn that it can reproduce traditional fear, foster witchcraft accusations against the vulnerable (children, the elderly, women) and blame spirits for social and political problems.
Missionary and Reformed critics see syncretism with traditional religion.
Prosperity-oriented deliverance can exploit the poor.
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/resp: African theologians answer that the gospel must be translated into African categories (Sanneh, Bediako) and that Christ’s victory frees from fear rather than feeding it.
Churches and theologians increasingly campaign against child-witch accusations.
positions/african-spiritual-warfare/cons: Central to African Christianity’s growth and identity.
Exported through African diaspora churches worldwide.
positions/strategic-level-spiritual-warf: High-ranking demonic powers hold sway over particular territories, cities and people groups; through research (“spiritual mapping”), identificational repentance and focused prayer, Christians can bind these spirits and open regions to the gospel.
Satan delegates territorial spirits to blind whole populations (2 Corinthians 4:4).
Spiritual mapping identifies strongholds; intercessors pray against them.
Breakthroughs in places such as Argentina followed such warfare.

Developed in the late 1980s-1990s by C. Peter Wagner (Fuller Seminary), George Otis Jr., Cindy Jacobs and the AD2000 United Prayer Track, drawing on reports from the Argentine revival (Carlos Annacondia, Omar Cabrera); it fed into the New Apostolic Reformation.
It takes seriously biblical hints of territorial powers.
It energises prayer and urban evangelism.
Practitioners report correlations between focused prayer and spiritual openness.
Biblical scholars (Arnold, Lowe) argue that the New Testament never instructs believers to identify or confront territorial spirits, only to resist the devil personally and proclaim the gospel.
The Lausanne statement (1993) warned against speculative mapping and quasi-animistic thinking.
Claims of measurable results have been questioned, and naming spirits can stigmatise local cultures.
Wagner answered that SLSW is an extension of ordinary intercession and that missionary experience reveals what Scripture implies.
Some practitioners moderated their claims and emphasised repentance and unity rather than naming spirits.
Shaped 1990s prayer movements (prayer walks, Transformations videos).
Became a foundation of the New Apostolic Reformation and later “Seven Mountains” teaching.
positions/demythologized-powers/oneLine: The New Testament’s demons, angels and cosmic powers belong to an ancient mythological world-picture; their meaning must be interpreted existentially as the forces that hold human existence in bondage, from which the kerygma calls us to authentic faith.
positions/demythologized-powers/coreClai: Modern people cannot believe in a three-storey universe populated by spirits.
Myth expresses human self-understanding, not objective description.
The cross and resurrection call to decision, freeing us from inauthentic existence.
The aim is to remove the false scandal of myth so the true scandal of the cross remains.
positions/demythologized-powers/origin: Proposed by Rudolf Bultmann in “New Testament and Mythology” (1941), building on liberal theology’s scepticism and Heidegger’s existentialism; widely debated in Germany and beyond into the 1960s.
positions/demythologized-powers/stronges: It removes obstacles that make Christianity seem incredible to modern people.
It locates the meaning of the powers in real human experience of bondage.
It keeps the focus on the kerygma rather than speculative demonology.
Barth, conservative scholars and Global South Christians argue it imposes a modern Western world-view on Scripture.
Critics note that the gospels’ exorcisms are integral to Jesus’ ministry and cannot be detached.
Majority-world Christianity, for which spirits are real, sees it as parochial.
positions/demythologized-powers/response: Bultmann answered that he sought to interpret myth, not eliminate it, and that faith must not depend on outdated cosmology.
Followers argue that existential interpretation does justice to the powers’ grip on human life.
positions/demythologized-powers/conseque: Prompted Wink’s and others’ reinterpretation of the powers and a later counter-reaction.
positions/powers-as-structures/name: The powers as structures (Wink; Christus Victor reading)
positions/powers-as-structures/oneLine: The New Testament “principalities and powers” are the spiritual interiority of real institutions, ideologies and systems; they are created good, fallen and to be redeemed, and Christ’s cross exposes and disarms them, calling the church to nonviolent resistance.
positions/powers-as-structures/coreClaim: Powers are neither mere myth nor free-floating demons, but the spirit of concrete structures.
They are good (created in Christ), fallen (idolatrous) and redeemable.
The cross unmasks and defeats the powers (Colossians 2:15).
The church engages the powers by naming, unmasking and nonviolent resistance.
positions/powers-as-structures/origin: Anticipated by Hendrik Berkhof (Christ and the Powers, 1953), John Howard Yoder and William Stringfellow; developed by Walter Wink’s Powers trilogy (1984-92); related to Aulén’s Christus Victor and to liberation theology.
positions/powers-as-structures/strongest: It holds together the biblical reality of the powers and the modern experience of systemic evil.
It gives Christus Victor atonement a social and political application.
It grounds Christian nonviolent action (civil rights, anti-apartheid).
Evangelical and Pentecostal critics argue it reduces personal demons to social forces, effectively demythologising.
Some biblical scholars argue Paul’s powers are personal spiritual beings.
Others say it can politicise the gospel.
positions/powers-as-structures/responses: Wink replied that his view rejects both reductionist materialism and supernaturalist dualism, affirming the powers’ spiritual reality as the “withinness” of institutions.
Supporters point to the cross as both personal and political victory.
positions/powers-as-structures/consequen: Influential in peace churches, mainline social ethics and nonviolent activism.
Shaped nonviolent and Christus Victor atonement theology.
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/oneLi: The late medieval and early modern theory, now repudiated by all churches, that witches had made a pact with the devil, flew to sabbaths, worshipped him and harmed neighbours by magic, constituting a crime to be prosecuted with torture and death.
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/coreC: Witches made explicit pacts with the devil and were organised in a conspiracy.
Women were held to be especially susceptible.
Denying witchcraft was itself suspected of heresy.
Secular and church courts should prosecute it severely, with torture.
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/keyTe: Exodus 22:18 (“thou shalt not suffer a witch to live”)
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/origi: Assembled in the 15th century from scholastic demonology, heresy trials and folk magic (Formicarius 1437; Summis desiderantes 1484; Malleus Maleficarum 1486); peaked c.1560-1660 in Catholic and Protestant lands, with perhaps 40,000-60,000 executions in Europe, about three-quarters of them women; spread to New England (Salem, 1692).
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/stron: Its proponents believed they were obeying biblical commands (Exodus 22:18) and protecting communities from real harm.
It drew on respected theological authorities on demonic power.
It responded, in their view, to confessions and testimonies of victims.

Contemporaries such as Johann Weyer (1563), Reginald Scot (1584), Friedrich Spee (1631) and the Spanish inquisitor Alonso de Salazar Frías (1611) showed that confessions were produced by torture and that accusations were unreliable.
Modern historians see the hunts as products of social stress, misogyny, legal procedure and religious conflict.
Christians today regard them as a grave betrayal of justice and of the gospel.
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/respo: There is no modern defence of the practice; churches have repented of it (e.g. later exonerations at Salem, apologies by church leaders).
Historians note that the Roman and Spanish Inquisitions were often more sceptical than secular courts, and that sceptics within the churches helped end the hunts.
positions/witch-hunting-demonology/conse: Tens of thousands of executions, mostly of women.
Left a lasting legacy of suspicion toward demonology and fuelled Enlightenment critiques of religion.
Witchcraft accusations continue in parts of Africa, Asia and Papua New Guinea, where churches are divided between fuelling and opposing them.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/oneLine: Scripture, rightly understood, gives the devil no power to act physically in the world; possession, witchcraft and spectral harms are superstitions, and God alone governs nature.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/coreClai: God’s providence leaves no room for devils acting in nature.
Biblical demon language is accommodated or metaphorical.
Witchcraft beliefs cause injustice and dishonour God.
Reason and Scripture together dispel superstition.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/origin: Developed by Balthasar Bekker (The World Bewitched, 1691) using Cartesian dualism, following earlier sceptics (Johann Weyer, Reginald Scot); continued in Enlightenment and liberal theology.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/stronges: It helped end the witch trials and the injustices they caused.
It affirms God’s sole sovereignty over creation.
It takes the accommodated character of biblical language seriously.
Orthodox Reformed contemporaries deposed Bekker for denying biblical teaching on Satan.
Critics argue it subordinates Scripture to Cartesian philosophy.
Global South Christians see it as Western rationalism blind to spiritual realities.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/response: Bekker’s defenders saw him as more biblical than his opponents in exalting God’s providence.
Later liberal theologians argued his scepticism was vindicated by science.
positions/bekker-disenchantment/conseque: Contributed to the decline of witch prosecutions in the Dutch Republic and beyond.
A forerunner of modern Western Christian scepticism about demons.
